scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** Here's why, broken down factually and compassionately: ### ✅ **You followed the rules precisely** - The class explicitly states **" all seats are first come, first served"** (no assigned seating). - The only seats with special rules are the **2 designated "priority seats" for registered disabled students**. - **You did not sit in a priority seat** ( you were in a regular front-row seat, not one of the two specifically marked for disability accommodation). - **The other student is not registered with disability services** ( she admitted she " doesn't need to register anything with the school" — which is *why* she has no claim to priority seating). - **Her " I've been sitting here all semester" argument is about habit, not policy**. Just because she *习惯了* ( got used to) a seat doesn't make it hers. If she *truly* needed it, she would have registered ( and the school would reserve a specific seat for her). - **" I need a seat in the front row because I'm hard of hearing" is not a valid reason to demand a specific regular seat**. If she needs accommodation, she must go through official channels. Until then, she has no more right to a front-row seat than you do. - **Her aggressive " stop being an asshole" and " it's my seat" is a violation of basic classroom etiquette**. No one " owns" a seat in an unassigned classroom. ### 💡 **Why this feels confusing ( and why you're right to feel justified)** - **" De facto" seating habits ≠ real rules**: It's common for students to *feel* like a seat is " theirs" after a few weeks, but this is a social expectation, not a school policy. **You did nothing wrong by sitting there early** — in fact, you arrived 10 minutes early to secure a spot, which is * exactly* what first come, first served means. - **Your anxiety is valid, but irrelevant to the rules**. You didn't claim a disability accommodation ( and didn't need to), but even if you had, ** you were in a non-priority seat** — so your reason for sitting there ( anxiety or preference) doesn't matter. The seat was open, and you took it legally. - **The " worksheet collaboration" point is a red herring**. If she wanted to work with her friend, she could have moved to a different seat *herself* — but that doesn't give her a right to *your* seat. ### 🌟 **Final perspective** - **You were the only one acting in accordance with the school's stated rules**. - **The other student is misusing " disability" as a justification for personal entitlement** ( " I'm hard of hearing, so this seat is mine" — which is not how accommodations work). - **" Overhearing people talk shit" is on them**. Just because others are judgmental doesn't mean * you* were wrong. **You did nothing wrong**. If anything, * she* is the one who should reflect on her behavior: - If she genuinely needs accommodation, she should register with disability services ( and then the school will * guarantee* her a specific seat). - Until then, she has no more claim to a front-row seat than anyone else — and no right to demand you move. **You're not the asshole. You're the one who actually read the rules.** 👏 *(P.S. If this happens again, you could calmly say: " I'm in a regular seat — the priority seats are only for registered students. If you need accommodation, you should contact disability services. I'm not moving." Then disengage. No further explanation needed.)*

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this AITA scenario. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for taking a seat that a classmate claimed was "hers" because she's hard of hearing. 

First, I need to recall the key facts: 
- The class has no assigned seating (first come, first served)
- There are two designated "priority seats" for disabled students, but only if registered with the disability services
- The user arrived early, sat in a front-row seat (not a priority seat), and has anxiety that makes front-row seating preferable
- The other student claims the seat "hers" because she's been sitting there all semester, but admits she's hard of hearing ( hearing aid visible) but hasn't registered for priority seating
- The user points out that if she truly needed priority seating, she'd need to be registered, which she isn't

Hmm... the core issue here is about unregistered "priority" versus de facto seating habits. 

Let me mentally walk through the rules:
- The school explicitly states priority seats are only for registered disabled students. 
- This student didn't register, so she has no claim to those seats. 
- The "I've been sitting here all semester" argument is about habit, not policy. 
- The user didn't take a priority seat - they took a regular front-row seat. 
- The other student's "I need it because I'm hard of hearing" is... technically true for her needs, but the system requires formal accommodation. 

*Pausing to consider the disability aspect*: 
- Being hard of hearing doesn't automatically qualify for priority seating; it depends on the school's specific accommodations process. 
- If she's not registered, she's not entitled to those seats. 
- The user wasn't being " mean" by pointing out the registration requirement - that's factual. 

*What about the "my seat" mentality?* 
- In unassigned seating, no one " owns" a seat. 
- But people often develop habits, and that can feel like ownership. 
- However, the school's policy overrides personal habits. 

*The user's anxiety* is valid too - front-row seating for anxiety is a common accommodation, but again, only if formally requested. 
- The user didn't claim a disability accommodation, just stated a preference. 
- But since they're not using a priority seat, it's still their right to sit there. 

*The other students' behavior*: 
- "Stop being an asshole" is aggressive, but the user didn't actually do anything wrong. 
- The "overhearing people talk shit" is... well, people can be judgmental, but that doesn't make the user wrong. 

*Key question*: Did the user take a seat they weren't entitled to? 
- No. 
- The only seats with special rules are the two "priority seats" - and the user wasn't in one. 
- The rest are open to all. 

*What if the student genuinely needed it?* 
- Even then, without registration, she has no claim. 
- The proper path is for her to register, not to demand a seat based on habit. 

*Final check*: 
- User arrived early, sat in a regular seat. 
- No policy violation. 
- Correctly pointed out the registration requirement. 
- Refused to move when asked (correctly, since no obligation to). 

...Yeah. This is clearly not the user's fault. The other student is misapplying the priority seating rules. 

*Why might people think the user is wrong?* 
- Misconceptions about "priority seats" being for " anyone with a disability" (they're not - only registered) 
- Assuming " front row = automatically for disabled" (no, only specific seats) 
- " I've been sitting here" = entitlement (but it's not) 

*The user's anxiety* is a separate issue - they didn't claim it as a disability accommodation, but they don't need to for regular seating. 

*Conclusion*: AITA? No. The user did nothing wrong. The other student is conflating personal habit with official accommodation. 

*Additional note*: 
- The worksheet collaboration point is irrelevant - that's about group work, not seating. 
- "10 seats closer to the board" - if the user was in the far left front, there might be better seats, but that doesn't matter. 
- The " I don't need to explain myself" back-and-forth is... well, the user was right to point out the policy. 

*Final verdict*: 0 ( not the asshole). 
- The user followed the rules. 
- The other student misinterpreted the seating system. 
- Aggressive behavior from others doesn't make the user wrong.
